title: Health, Disease and Immunity
seo_title: Anatomy and Physiology 12: Health, Disease and Immunity Worksheets (BC Curriculum)
standard_text: Lifestyle choices and environmental factors affect health: pathogens and disease, the immune system, vaccines, and the effects of lifestyle (diet, smoking, drugs, exercise) on body systems. (summary of BC's Curriculum, Anatomy and Physiology 12)
meta_desc: Free Anatomy and Physiology 12 worksheets (BC Curriculum): pathogens, immunity, vaccines and lifestyle. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: The immune system defends against pathogens.
key_sub: Lifestyle choices affect the health of organ systems.
body_html:
How to think about it

Pathogens include bacteria, viruses, fungi and protists. Innate (non-specific) defences include skin, mucus, inflammation and phagocytes. The adaptive immune system uses B cells (antibodies) and T cells and has memory, so a second infection is fought faster.

Vaccines create memory cells without causing the disease; herd immunity protects people who cannot be vaccinated. Smoking damages the lungs and blood vessels, a poor diet and inactivity raise the risk of heart disease and type 2 diabetes, and alcohol and drugs affect the liver and nervous system.

Example

Which cells make antibodies?

B for…

Answer: B cells (plasma cells)

Example

Why is the second response to a pathogen faster?

The body remembers.

Answer: memory cells

Common mistakes

  • Thinking antibiotics work on viruses.
  • Thinking vaccines contain the full, live disease.
  • Thinking only genes decide health.

faq.q: How does smoking affect the lungs?
faq.a: It damages cilia and alveoli and can cause cancer and emphysema.

items.q: Which organism causes ascariasis?
items.e: Ascariasis: Ascaris (roundworm).

items.q: What is a pathogen?
c: a toxin made by the body
an organism or agent that causes disease
items.e: Most microorganisms are harmless.

items.q: What type of pathogen causes tobacco mosaic virus (TMV)?
items.e: Viruses, bacteria, fungi and protists.

items.q: What type of pathogen causes measles?
items.e: Viruses, bacteria, fungi and protists.

items.q: How is tobacco mosaic virus (TMV) spread?
items.e: Know how to stop the spread.

items.q: What does the basic reproduction number R₀ tell epidemiologists?
c: the number of vaccines needed per person
the number of days a disease lasts
the number of deaths from a disease
the average number of people one infected person infects in a fully susceptible population
items.e: If R is below 1, the outbreak shrinks.

items.q: Which symptom is linked to measles?
c: a mosaic pattern of discoloured leaves
a red skin rash and fever
flu-like illness, then damage to the immune system
items.e: Symptoms help diagnosis.

items.q: Why is the secondary immune response faster and stronger?
c: memory cells made in the first response recognize the antigen quickly
the pathogen is weaker the second time
items.e: This is the basis of vaccination.

items.q: Which symptom is linked to salmonella food poisoning?
c: a mosaic pattern of discoloured leaves
a thick yellow or green discharge and pain when urinating
flu-like illness, then damage to the immune system
fever, stomach cramps, vomiting and diarrhoea
items.e: Symptoms help diagnosis.

items.q: Which symptom is linked to tobacco mosaic virus (TMV)?
c: purple or black spots on leaves
a red skin rash and fever
a mosaic pattern of discoloured leaves
items.e: Symptoms help diagnosis.

items.q: What type of pathogen causes rose black spot?
items.e: Viruses, bacteria, fungi and protists.

items.q: How is salmonella food poisoning spread?
c: spores carried by wind or water
sexual contact and exchange of body fluids
items.e: Know how to stop the spread.

items.q: Which disease is caused by Salmonella typhi?
items.e: Typhoid: Salmonella typhi.

items.q: What is the role of cytotoxic (killer) T cells?
c: destroying body cells infected by viruses
items.e: Helper T cells activate B and cytotoxic T cells.

items.q: Which disease is caused by Ascaris (roundworm)?
items.e: Ascariasis: Ascaris (roundworm).

items.q: How is HIV spread?
c: sexual contact and exchange of body fluids
spores carried by wind or water
items.e: Know how to stop the spread.

items.q: Which symptom is linked to rose black spot?
c: fever, stomach cramps, vomiting and diarrhoea
purple or black spots on leaves
a thick yellow or green discharge and pain when urinating
items.e: Symptoms help diagnosis.

items.q: Which types of pathogens cause disease?
c: viruses, bacteria, fungi, protists, parasites and prions
items.e: Prions are misfolded proteins.

items.q: How is malaria spread?
c: sexual contact and exchange of body fluids
items.e: Know how to stop the spread.

items.q: How is measles spread?
c: sexual contact and exchange of body fluids
items.e: Know how to stop the spread.

items.q: What is an antigen?
c: a molecule, usually on a pathogen's surface, recognized by the immune system
a protein made by B cells
items.e: Antibodies bind to antigens.

items.q: Which white blood cells mature in the thymus?
items.e: B cells mature in the bone marrow.

items.q: What is clonal selection?
c: the B or T cell with the matching receptor is selected and divides
items.e: Then clonal expansion happens.

items.q: Which disease is caused by a bacterium?
items.e: Bacteria can be treated with antibiotics.

items.q: Which cells make antibodies?
items.e: Plasma cells are made from B cells.

items.q: Which cells make antibodies?
items.e: T cells give cell-mediated immunity.

items.q: What is a monoclonal antibody?
c: an antibody made from a single clone of B cells
items.e: Used in pregnancy tests and targeted drugs.

items.q: What is the second line of defence?
c: the non-specific innate response: inflammation, fever and phagocytes
items.e: It responds to any pathogen.

items.q: Why do antibiotics not work against HIV?
c: viruses have no cell wall or ribosomes for antibiotics to target
items.e: Antiretroviral drugs are used instead.

items.q: How do plants defend themselves against pathogens?
c: waxy cuticles, thick cell walls and chemicals such as antimicrobial compounds
items.e: Some plants also close stomata or kill infected cells.

items.q: Which measure reduces the spread of a respiratory virus?
c: hand washing, masks and staying home when sick
items.e: These reduce transmission.

items.q: What is an autoimmune disease?
c: a disease in which the immune system attacks the body's own cells
items.e: e.g. rheumatoid arthritis.

items.q: What is an ethical issue with vaccines?
c: testing may involve animals or there may be side effects
items.e: There are also questions about compulsory vaccination.

items.q: What is active immunity?
c: your own immune system makes antibodies after exposure to an antigen
items.e: It gives long-lasting memory.

items.q: What is an antibody?
c: a protein that binds to a specific antigen
items.e: Made by plasma cells.

items.q: Why might a transplanted organ be rejected?
c: the organ has no blood supply
the body recognizes its antigens as foreign
items.e: Immunosuppressant drugs reduce the risk.

items.q: What do cytotoxic T cells do?
c: kill infected body cells by making holes in them (perforin)
items.e: Part of the cellular response.

items.q: How does a vaccine work?
c: it exposes the immune system to an antigen so memory cells form without causing the disease
it kills all bacteria in the body
it gives the person antibodies for life
items.e: This is artificial active immunity.

items.q: What is a zoonosis?
c: a disease that spreads from animals to people
items.e: Hendra virus spreads from flying foxes via horses.

items.q: What is the cellular response?
items.e: T cells respond to antigens on cells.

items.q: How does a vaccine give protection?
c: it contains antigens that cause memory cells to be made
items.e: A later infection gives a fast secondary response.

items.q: Which part of the body's defences does this: “Move mucus with trapped pathogens up to the throat”?
c: hairs and mucus in the nose
cilia in the trachea and bronchi
items.e: First and second lines of defence.

items.q: What is inflammation?
c: swelling, redness and heat as blood vessels widen and white blood cells move to an infected area
items.e: Mast cells release histamine.

items.q: How do antitoxins help defend the body?
c: They trap particles that may contain pathogens.
It kills pathogens in food and drink.
They neutralize toxins made by bacteria.
items.e: First and second lines of defence.

items.q: Which part of the body's defences does this: “Trap particles that may contain pathogens”?
c: hairs and mucus in the nose
cilia in the trachea and bronchi
items.e: First and second lines of defence.

items.q: What is an antigen?
c: a type of white blood cell
a protein made by B cells
a molecule that triggers an immune response
items.e: Usually a protein on the surface of a cell or virus.

items.q: What do plasma cells make?
items.e: Plasma cells come from B lymphocytes.

items.q: How do phagocytes (white blood cells) help defend the body?
c: It acts as a barrier and makes antimicrobial secretions.
It kills pathogens in food and drink.
They move mucus with trapped pathogens up to the throat.
items.e: First and second lines of defence.

items.q: Which disease is caused by a fungus?
items.e: Fungi also cause many plant diseases.

items.q: What does an antibody's variable region do?
items.e: Its shape is complementary to the antigen.

items.q: How do hairs and mucus in the nose help defend the body?
c: They trap particles that may contain pathogens.
It kills pathogens in food and drink.
They attach to antigens on pathogens so they can be destroyed.
items.e: First and second lines of defence.

items.q: How do antibodies help defend the body?
c: They move mucus with trapped pathogens up to the throat.
It acts as a barrier and makes antimicrobial secretions.
It kills pathogens in food and drink.
They attach to antigens on pathogens so they can be destroyed.
items.e: First and second lines of defence.

items.q: How does acid in the stomach help defend the body?
c: They move mucus with trapped pathogens up to the throat.
It kills pathogens in food and drink.
It acts as a barrier and makes antimicrobial secretions.
items.e: First and second lines of defence.

items.q: Why is contact tracing used in an outbreak?
c: to find and isolate people who may have been infected before they spread the disease
items.e: It reduces transmission.

items.q: What is herd immunity?
c: when enough people are vaccinated that a disease cannot spread easily
items.e: It protects unvaccinated people too.

items.q: Which part of the body's defences does this: “Attach to antigens on pathogens so they can be destroyed”?
items.e: First and second lines of defence.

items.q: Which part of the body's defences does this: “Acts as a barrier and makes antimicrobial secretions”?
c: cilia in the trachea and bronchi
items.e: First and second lines of defence.

items.q: What is antigenic variability?
c: a pathogen's antigens change, so memory cells do not recognize them
items.e: This is why flu vaccines change each year.

items.q: Which part of the body's defences does this: “Engulf and digest pathogens”?
items.e: First and second lines of defence.

items.q: Which part of the body's defences does this: “Neutralize toxins made by bacteria”?
c: cilia in the trachea and bronchi
items.e: First and second lines of defence.

items.q: How does a vaccine work?
c: It contains dead or inactive pathogens, so white blood cells make antibodies and memory cells without illness.
It contains antibodies from another person.
items.e: Fast response next time.

items.q: Why do antibiotics not work against viruses?
c: Viruses live inside cells, and antibiotics only kill bacteria.
items.e: Use antivirals or let the immune system fight.

items.q: How does antibiotic resistance develop?
c: antibiotics make bacteria change on purpose
bacteria with resistance alleles survive antibiotic treatment and multiply
items.e: Finishing courses and limiting use slow it.

items.q: What are Koch's postulates used for?
c: showing that a particular microorganism causes a particular disease
items.e: The pathogen must be isolated and cause the disease again.

items.q: Why are antibiotics not used to treat viral infections?
c: antibiotics target bacterial structures such as cell walls and ribosomes, which viruses do not have
viruses are not living, so they cannot be infected
items.e: Antivirals target viral processes.

items.q: Which organism causes filariasis?
items.e: Filariasis: Wuchereria.

items.q: Which disease is caused by Wuchereria?
items.e: Filariasis: Wuchereria.

items.q: What is an allergy?
c: an exaggerated immune response to an allergen such as pollen or dust
items.e: IgE antibodies and histamine are involved.

items.q: Which plant produces digitalis, used to treat heart conditions?
items.e: Aspirin came from willow.

items.q: What do painkillers do?
c: relieve symptoms but do not kill pathogens
items.e: Treat symptoms only.

items.q: Which test is widely used to diagnose AIDS?
items.e: It detects antibodies to HIV.

items.q: Which disease is caused by Plasmodium?
items.e: Malaria: Plasmodium.

items.q: Which is part of the body's first line of defence?
items.e: These are physical and chemical barriers.

items.q: What is passive immunity?
c: receiving antibodies made by another organism, such as from mother to baby
making your own antibodies after infection
items.e: It gives short-term protection.

items.q: In a drug trial, what is a double-blind trial?
c: Neither the patients nor the doctors know who has the drug or the placebo.
items.e: Avoids bias.

items.q: Who discovered penicillin?
items.e: From Penicillium mold.

items.q: How does antibiotic resistance spread?
c: Resistant bacteria survive treatment and reproduce, so resistant strains become common.
items.e: Natural selection.

items.q: Which mosquito transmits malaria?
items.e: Aedes spreads dengue and chikungunya.

items.q: Which toxin causes the chill and high fever of malaria?
items.e: It is released when red blood cells burst.

items.q: What is the main cause of cancer at the cell level?
c: loss of contact inhibition, so cells divide uncontrollably
items.e: Carcinogens can cause it.

items.q: What is a drug?
c: a substance that changes the way the body or mind works
items.e: Medicinal or recreational.

items.q: Which substance in cigarette smoke: they irritate the airways and damage the alveoli.
items.e: Nicotine addicts; tar causes cancer; carbon monoxide reduces oxygen carried.

items.q: Why do antibiotics not cure colds?
c: Colds are caused by viruses, and antibiotics only kill bacteria.
items.e: Use antibiotics only when needed.
